---
redu_schema: 2
repo: https://github.com/denho/faved
plan:
  tool: deploy_compose
  image: denho/faved:2.10.0
  port: 8080
  vm: m1.medium
  flavor_id: "3"
  database: none. Faved is SQLite-only, so do NOT provision a managed database for it
  hourly_cost_gbp: 0.0278
bootstrap:
  mcp: claude mcp add --transport http redu «REDACTED:env:78213b90» --client-id redu-mcp
  mcp_codex: codex mcp add redu --url «REDACTED:env:78213b90» --oauth-client-id redu-mcp
  source: faved
quirks:
  - "⛔ DO NOT PROVISION A MANAGED DATABASE FOR THIS APP. It would bill on its own VM forever and Faved would never open a connection to it. SQLite is the only backend that exists in the codebase: Config.php:6-14 builds a path to storage/<DB_NAME or faved>.db and SetupDatabaseController.php:36 opens it with a sqlite PDO. There is no Postgres or MySQL driver, no DATABASE_URL, no dialect setting. So deploy_compose gets NO database argument, and the usual 'wire the managed Postgres or lose everything' quirk is replaced by the volume quirk below, which carries exactly the same consequence."
  - "⛔⛔ MOUNT A VOLUME ON /var/www/html/storage OR YOU LOSE EVERYTHING ON THE NEXT REDEPLOY. That one directory holds the SQLite database AND the cached preview images (Config.php:7,9,17-20 and Dockerfile.build:61-64, where the image creates it owned by www-data). There is no second copy anywhere: no managed database, no object store. A redeploy without that volume produces a perfectly healthy container showing the first-run setup wizard, which is what losing every bookmark looks like from the outside. Also keep a volume on /tmp, as upstream's compose does: PHP sessions live there, so without it every restart signs you out (the cookie is faved-session with a 7-day lifetime, Config.php:30-38)."
  - "⛔⛔ WHO BECOMES THE ADMINISTRATOR, AND WHEN: THE FIRST PERSON TO CREATE THE ACCOUNT, AND UNTIL THEY DO, THERE IS NO AUTHENTICATION ON ANYTHING. Verified in framework/Middlewares/AuthenticationMiddleware.php:34-43: the middleware returns early, letting the request straight through, when the database file is missing OR the users table is empty. So on a fresh public hostname an anonymous visitor can list, create and delete bookmarks and tags, run the importers, and above all POST to /api/settings/user and claim the only account the instance will ever have. Faved's own setup wizard even offers a \"Skip for now\" button on that step (frontend/src/pages/SetupAuth.tsx:23-25), so an operator can leave it open by accident. CLAIM THE ACCOUNT AS PART OF THE DEPLOY, before you hand the URL over, using the script in this document. Nothing else closes the window."
  - "REGISTRATION CLOSES ITSELF, PERMANENTLY, AND THERE IS NO SETTING TO SET. controllers/UserCreateController.php:23-33 refuses a second account with HTTP 400 'User has been created already'. Faved is a single-user app: one account, no roles, no invitations, no admin panel. So the answer to 'is registration open after the first account' is no, structurally. That also means the only window that ever exists is the gap between the hostname resolving and you creating the account, which is why the claim belongs in the deploy and not in the handover notes."
  - "THE CLAIM IS TWO CALLS, AND THE SECOND ONE NEEDS A CSRF PAIR. The container does NOT create its schema at start: POST /api/setup/database does (SetupDatabaseController.php:17-55), which is what the wizard's first screen calls. Until then every API route answers HTTP 424 with 'Database not found. Please set up the database first.' Then POST /api/settings/user creates the account. Both are non-GET, and framework/Middlewares/CSRFMiddleware.php:22-45 requires the CSRF-TOKEN cookie to be echoed back in an X-CSRF-TOKEN header, with the token held in the PHP session. So use one cookie jar: GET first to be issued the pair, then POST with the header. Skipping this gives HTTP 403 'CSRF token validation failed', which is easy to misread as the app refusing the signup."
  - "PASSWORD AND USERNAME RULES, SO THE CLAIM DOES NOT FAIL ON VALIDATION: the username must match [a-zA-Z0-9_] with no dots, dashes or e-mail addresses (framework/helper-functions.php:83-93), and the password must be at least 6 characters and be repeated in a confirm_password field or the request is rejected (framework/helper-functions.php:56-80). Generate an alphanumeric value of 24 characters or more, so there is nothing to escape in JSON or in the shell, and send the body on stdin so it never appears in ps."
  - "PORT 80 IN THE CONTAINER, 8080 ON THE VM. apache-conf/faved.conf:1 declares one <VirtualHost *:80> and the image has no other listener; upstream's compose publishes it as ${PORT:-8080}:80. Write the mapping literally as 8080:80 in your compose rather than relying on the PORT variable, because deploy_compose appends its own variables to the project .env and you do not want the published port depending on what is or is not in that file. Pass port 8080 to deploy_compose."
  - "⛔ DELETE THE 443 PORT, THE certbot-conf VOLUME AND THE apache-conf VOLUME from upstream's compose. The image ships certbot (Dockerfile.build:33) and the compose mounts /etc/letsencrypt and /etc/apache2/sites-enabled so you can terminate TLS inside the container. On redu you must not: redu terminates TLS at its own proxy with the wildcard certificate for the hostname it gave you, and asking Let's Encrypt for a per-host certificate for a .redu.cloud name burns a rate limit that is shared across every deploy on the platform and cannot be lifted early. The apache-conf volume is worth removing for a second reason: a named volume is seeded from the image the first time it is used and never again, so it would pin the vhost config of whichever image version you booted first and silently keep it across upgrades."
  - "WHAT AN ANONYMOUS REQUEST CAN REACH, BEFORE THE ACCOUNT EXISTS: everything. GET and POST /api/items, the tag routes, POST /api/import/bookmarks and /api/import/pocket, /api/url/fetch-metadata, /content/fetch-image and POST /api/settings/user itself. AFTER the account exists: nothing but the login page and its POST /api/auth/login, since every other controller is behind the middleware and answers 401 (framework/Exceptions/UnauthorizedException.php). One piece of genuinely good news, verified rather than assumed: the two routes that fetch a user-supplied URL server-side are behind an SSRF guard that rejects private and link-local addresses and pins the connection to the resolved IP, so even in the unclaimed window they are not a probe into your own private network (init.php:42-58, utils/safe-http-functions.php:129-147)."

# Self-host Faved on redu

A fast, private bookmark manager with nested tags: one PHP container, its SQLite database on a
persistent volume, a public HTTPS URL, and no database VM to pay for.

## What this deploys

- **Faved** from the official image, pinned, on one m1.medium VM. Port 80 in the container,
  published on 8080.
- A volume on `/var/www/html/storage`, which holds **the database itself** and every cached
  preview image.
- A volume on `/tmp`, which holds PHP sessions, so a restart does not sign you out.
- A public hostname on `*.redu.cloud` with TLS.

About GBP 0.028/hour, roughly GBP 20 a month. Inside the no-card free trial. Delete it any time.

## No managed database, on purpose

Faved is SQLite-only: the database is a single file under `storage/`, and there is no Postgres
or MySQL driver anywhere in the codebase. So this is one of the few entries in this library that
provisions no database VM, which is why it is cheap. The trade is that **the volume is the whole
story**: lose it and you lose everything, exactly as if you had lost a database.

## Deploy

Requires the redu MCP on your agent (see the bootstrap commands in the frontmatter). Then, from a
directory containing this file:

    Read redu.md and deploy Faved on redu.

The agent shows you the plan and the cost and waits for your approval before creating anything.

## The compose

Upstream's own compose is close to right, but it publishes 443, mounts `/etc/letsencrypt` and
mounts a volume over Apache's `sites-enabled`. redu terminates TLS at its proxy, so all three
come out:

```yaml
name: faved
services:
  faved:

SOURCE IS EITHER GIT OR UPLOAD, NEVER BOTH. For code that is not pushed, or is private, or needs fixing first: write the files locally, call prepare_upload, run the tar+curl block it returns, then pass the source_token and NO repo. ⚠️ prepare_upload EXCLUDES .env from the tarball by design, so secrets have to reach the VM another way (pass them to the deploy call, not in the tree).

A MANAGED DATABASE IS A SECOND VM WITH ITS OWN HOURLY RATE, and delete_deployment deliberately LEAVES IT BEHIND so your data survives the app. That means a teardown that stops at delete_deployment keeps billing a database nobody can reach. Call delete_database too, and say so to the user before either.

A MANAGED POSTGRES SERVES EXACTLY ONE DATABASE. pg_hba is evaluated before role privileges, so being superuser does not help. An app that wants a second database needs a second managed server. This has broken deploys that otherwise looked healthy.

get_deployment RETURNS THE MERGED redu.md ONLY WHEN IT FITS ITS RESPONSE BUDGET. Over budget - which is normal for a mature recipe or any large app - it withholds redu_md_markdown and returns redu_md_last_deploy_block plus redu_md_deploy_log_line instead. That is NOT an error and must not be retried: apply those two edits to the file on disk and change nothing else.

⛔ THE MERGE NEVER WRITES A NEW QUIRK. Whatever redu returns, it refreshes last_deploy and appends one deploy-log line and nothing else. Every gotcha YOUR run discovered has to be typed into the quirks list by hand before you commit, or it is lost - and that list is the only part of the file that makes the next deploy cheaper.
⛔ NEVER WRITE A CREDENTIAL INTO redu.md. It is committed and read by the next person and the next agent. Names of variables, yes; their values, never. Hand secrets to the user in the session instead.

plan_deploy OVER-SIZES A PULLED COMPOSE STACK. Measured 8 times out of 8: declaring needs_compose makes it quote m1.large, roughly double the real requirement, because it cannot see that the images are pulled rather than built. Show the user the plan, but size from the app's real memory figure when you have one.

THE MANAGED DATABASE PASSWORD IS ON THE VM, NOT IN THE API. list_databases returns private_ip, port, db_name and db_user and DELIBERATELY NOT the password, so an agent that looks for it there finds nothing and starts guessing. The deploy writes the whole connection set into the compose project's .env on the app VM. Call get_env_keys for the NAMES first (no SSH, values never leave the VM); only if you need an actual VALUE, SSH in (get_ssh_command) and read that one key, `sudo grep '^PGPASSWORD=' /opt/app-src/.env`. ⚠️ That file is chmod 600 root:root so it needs sudo, and the database is on the PRIVATE network - reachable from the app VM, never from a laptop.

YOU CAN READ A DEPLOY VM WITHOUT SSHING INTO IT, and four tools do it: get_containers (what is running, health, restarts, crashed ones included), get_container_logs (what the app actually printed - the tool for 'deployed fine but does not work'), get_resource_usage (memory, disk, load, OOM kills) and get_env_keys (which variables got wired, by name). ⛔ get_instance_logs is the SERIAL CONSOLE and is not your app's logs; build_log stops when the build does. SSH is still yours for everything else - a shell on a real machine is the point, not a fallback. ⭐ MEASURED over 38 deploys: of 241 ssh escapes, 146 (61%) were exactly these four things, and the four tools were called 11 times. They are faster than a login, they cost the VM nothing extra (the reading is already cached), and reaching for ssh to run `docker ps` is the single most common wasted minute in a deploy.

⛔ THE PRIMARY SURFACE'S HOSTNAME COMES FROM THE TOP-LEVEL dname, NOT FROM expose[0].dname, WHICH IS SILENTLY DISCARDED. Extra expose entries DO keep the dname you give them, so the two behave differently and nothing tells you. If an app bakes its own public URL into config at boot (CPAD_MAIN_DOMAIN, allowed_origins, SITE_URL), generate the full `<label>-<8 lowercase letters/digits>.redu.cloud` form yourself and pass it as the TOP-LEVEL dname, which is used verbatim. Passing it on expose[0] instead gets you an app configured for a hostname redu never created, answering 200 on a name it does not believe is its own.

WEBSOCKETS WORK THROUGH THE PROXY WITH NO CONFIGURATION: every proxy host redu creates has upgrade enabled. Measured at the protocol level, HTTP/1.1 101 Switching Protocols with the subprotocol echoed back. ⚠️ TEST IT WITH `curl --http1.1`: plain curl negotiates HTTP/2, which has no Upgrade mechanism at all, so the app answers as an ordinary GET and the failure looks exactly like a proxy refusing to upgrade. Browsers use HTTP/1.1 for websockets regardless. Do not disable an app's realtime features on the strength of an HTTP/2 curl.

# Self-host Faved on redu

A fast, private bookmark manager with nested tags: one PHP container, its SQLite database on a
persistent volume, a public HTTPS URL, and no database VM to pay for.

## What this deploys

- **Faved** from the official image, pinned, on one m1.medium VM. Port 80 in the container,
  published on 8080.
- A volume on `/var/www/html/storage`, which holds **the database itself** and every cached
  preview image.
- A volume on `/tmp`, which holds PHP sessions, so a restart does not sign you out.
- A public hostname on `*.redu.cloud` with TLS.

About GBP 0.028/hour, roughly GBP 20 a month. Inside the no-card free trial. Delete it any time.

## No managed database, on purpose

Faved is SQLite-only: the database is a single file under `storage/`, and there is no Postgres
or MySQL driver anywhere in the codebase. So this is one of the few entries in this library that
provisions no database VM, which is why it is cheap. The trade is that **the volume is the whole
story**: lose it and you lose everything, exactly as if you had lost a database.

## Deploy

Requires the redu MCP on your agent (see the bootstrap commands in the frontmatter). Then, from a
directory containing this file:

    Read redu.md and deploy Faved on redu.

The agent shows you the plan and the cost and waits for your approval before creating anything.

## The compose

Upstream's own compose is close to right, but it publishes 443, mounts `/etc/letsencrypt` and
mounts a volume over Apache's `sites-enabled`. redu terminates TLS at its proxy, so all three
come out:

```yaml
name: faved
services:
  faved:
    image: denho/faved:2.10.0
    restart: unless-stopped
    working_dir: /var/www/html
    volumes:
      - storage:/var/www/html/storage/
      - temp-data:/tmp/
    ports:
      - "8080:80"
volumes:
  storage:
  temp-data:
```

No environment block: `DB_NAME` is the only variable the application reads and its default is
the right one.

## The three that actually break it

**Nobody owns it until somebody claims it.** Faved skips authentication entirely while the users
table is empty, so a fresh instance on a public hostname is wide open, and the first visitor to
post to `/api/settings/user` gets the only account it will ever have. Claim it during the
deploy.

**The volume.** `storage/` is the database. Without a volume the app comes up perfectly healthy
and shows the setup wizard, which is what a total loss looks like from outside.

**The schema is created over HTTP, not at boot.** Until `POST /api/setup/database` runs, every
route answers `424` with "Database not found". That is normal, not a broken deploy.

## Claim it, and prove the claim took

Run this the moment the deploy reports ready. It creates the schema, takes the single account,
proves the account can actually sign in, and then proves a second signup is refused **for the
right reason** rather than because a CSRF check happened to reject it.

```bash
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# Claim this Faved instance before anyone else can, and prove it.
#   ./claim-faved.sh faved-xxxxxxxx.redu.cloud
# Exit 0 = claimed and proven, 1 = someone else got there first, 2 = inconclusive.
set -eu
HOST="${1:?usage: claim-faved.sh <host>}"
USERNAME="${FAVED_USER:-owner}"
TMP=$(mktemp -d); trap 'rm -rf "$TMP"' EXIT
API="https://$HOST/api"
JAR="$TMP/jar1"

# Faved accepts a non-GET request only when the CSRF-TOKEN cookie it issued is echoed back in an
# X-CSRF-TOKEN header, and the token lives in the PHP session, so each stage shares one jar.
csrf() { awk '$6 == "CSRF-TOKEN" { print $7 }' "$JAR" | tail -n 1; }

# 1. GATE. Nothing below means anything until Faved itself is answering. redu's hostname returns
#    502 from its proxy for roughly the first 2.5 minutes while the container starts, and an error
#    page fails every assertion in a way that reads like a pass.
code=$(curl -sS -c "$JAR" -b "$JAR" -o "$TMP/user" -w '%{http_code}' \
  -H 'Accept: application/json' "$API/settings/user")
case "$code" in
  424) STATE=no-database ;;   # the schema has not been created yet. Expected on a fresh deploy.
  200) STATE=no-user ;;       # schema exists, no account yet: the instance is UNCLAIMED.
  401) echo "STOP: an account ALREADY EXISTS on this instance (HTTP 401)." >&2
       echo "  If you did not create it, someone else claimed it. Do not use it: delete the" >&2
       echo "  deployment and redeploy, then run this script immediately." >&2
       exit 1 ;;
  502) echo "INCONCLUSIVE: 502 from redu's proxy, the container is still starting. Re-run." >&2
       exit 2 ;;
  *)   echo "INCONCLUSIVE: /api/settings/user answered HTTP $code, which this script does not" >&2
       echo "  recognise. Do not assume the instance is safe." >&2
       exit 2 ;;
esac

# 2. POSITIVE CONTROL. Prove the body came from Faved and not from something else on this
#    hostname that happens to answer with the same status code.
if [ "$STATE" = "no-database" ]; then
  grep -q 'Database not found' "$TMP/user" || {
    echo "INCONCLUSIVE: HTTP 424 but not Faved's body." >&2; exit 2; }
else
  grep -q '"user"' "$TMP/user" || {
    echo "INCONCLUSIVE: HTTP 200 but not Faved's body." >&2; exit 2; }
fi
TOKEN=«REDACTED:assigned:3e91cfc3»
[ -n "$TOKEN" ] || {
  echo "INCONCLUSIVE: no CSRF-TOKEN cookie was issued, so nothing below could have worked." >&2
  exit 2; }
echo "OK: Faved is serving on $HOST, and it is UNCLAIMED right now."

# 3. Create the schema. The container does not do this at start; the wizard's first screen does.
code=$(curl -sS -c "$JAR" -b "$JAR" -o "$TMP/setup" -w '%{http_code}' \
  -X POST -H 'Accept: application/json' -H "X-CSRF-TOKEN: [REDACTED:value]" "$API/setup/database")
if [ "$code" != "200" ] && ! grep -q 'already exists' "$TMP/setup"; then
  echo "FAILED to create the database: HTTP $code" >&2; cat "$TMP/setup" >&2; exit 2
fi

# 4. Claim the one account. Alphanumeric only, so there is nothing to escape in JSON or the
#    shell, and the body goes in on stdin so it never shows up in ps.
SECRET=«REDACTED:assigned:08bdef6e» tr -dc 'A-Za-z0-9' < /dev/urandom | head -c 32)
TOKEN=«REDACTED:assigned:3e91cfc3»
code=$(printf '{"username":"%s","password":"[REDACTED:value]","confirm_password":"[REDACTED:value]"}' \
    "$USERNAME" "$SECRET" "$SECRET" \
  | curl -sS -c "$JAR" -b "$JAR" -o "$TMP/create" -w '%{http_code}' \
      -X POST -H 'Accept: application/json' -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
      -H "X-CSRF-TOKEN: [REDACTED:value]" --data-binary @- "$API/settings/user")
[ "$code" = "201" ] || {
  echo "FAILED to create the account: HTTP $code" >&2; cat "$TMP/create" >&2; exit 2; }

# 5. PROVE THE OUTCOME, not the status code: sign in from a clean session with those credentials.
JAR="$TMP/jar2"
curl -sS -c "$JAR" -o /dev/null -H 'Accept: application/json' "$API/settings/user"
TOKEN=«REDACTED:assigned:3e91cfc3»
code=$(printf '{"username":"%s","password":"[REDACTED:value]"}' "$USERNAME" "$SECRET" \
  | curl -sS -c "$JAR" -b "$JAR" -o "$TMP/login" -w '%{http_code}' \
      -X POST -H 'Accept: application/json' -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
      -H "X-CSRF-TOKEN: [REDACTED:value]" --data-binary @- "$API/auth/login")
if [ "$code" != "200" ] || ! grep -q '"success":true' "$TMP/login"; then
  echo "FAILED: the account exists but it cannot sign in (HTTP $code)." >&2
  cat "$TMP/login" >&2; exit 2
fi
echo "OK: signed in as $USERNAME, so the credentials are real."

# 6. Prove registration is CLOSED by behaviour, and for the right reason. A probe without a CSRF
#    token would be refused as a CSRF failure and would prove nothing at all, so this one carries
#    a valid token from a fresh anonymous session.
JAR="$TMP/jar3"
curl -sS -c "$JAR" -o /dev/null -H 'Accept: application/json' "$API/settings/user"
TOKEN=«REDACTED:assigned:3e91cfc3»
[ -n "$TOKEN" ] || { echo "INCONCLUSIVE: no CSRF cookie on the anonymous probe." >&2; exit 2; }
code=$(printf '{"username":"probe","password":"[REDACTED:value]","confirm_password":"[REDACTED:value]"}' "$SECRET" "$SECRET" \
  | curl -sS -c "$JAR" -b "$JAR" -o "$TMP/probe" -w '%{http_code}' \
      -X POST -H 'Accept: application/json' -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
      -H "X-CSRF-TOKEN: [REDACTED:value]" --data-binary @- "$API/settings/user")
if [ "$code" = "201" ]; then
  echo "FAIL: an anonymous request just created a SECOND account. Do not leave this running." >&2
  exit 1
fi
grep -q 'already' "$TMP/probe" || {
  echo "INCONCLUSIVE: the second signup was refused with HTTP $code, but not with the" >&2
  echo "  'User has been created already' answer this asserts on. A CSRF or routing failure" >&2
  echo "  refuses everything and would prove nothing here." >&2
  cat "$TMP/probe" >&2; exit 2; }
echo "OK: a second signup is refused as already created. Faved is single-user; the window is shut."

echo
echo "Sign in at https://$HOST as: $USERNAME"
printf 'The generated credential is: %s\n' "$SECRET"
echo "Put it in a password manager now. This is the only account this instance will ever have."
```

So the deploy isn't done at "ready": I immediately create the schema (`POST /api/setup/database`), claim the single account, prove it can sign in, and prove a second signup is refused. cat > claim-faved.sh <<'SCRIPTEOF'
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# Claim this Faved instance before anyone else can, and prove it.
#   ./claim-faved.sh faved-xxxxxxxx.redu.cloud
# Exit 0 = claimed and proven, 1 = someone else got there first, 2 = inconclusive.
set -eu
HOST="${1:?usage: claim-faved.sh <host>}"
USERNAME="${FAVED_USER:-owner}"
TMP=$(mktemp -d); trap 'rm -rf "$TMP"' EXIT
API="https://$HOST/api"
JAR="$TMP/jar1"

# Faved accepts a non-GET request only when the CSRF-TOKEN cookie it issued is echoed back in an
# X-CSRF-TOKEN header, and the token lives in the PHP session, so each stage shares one jar.
csrf() { awk '$6 == "CSRF-TOKEN" { print $7 }' "$JAR" | tail -n 1; }

# 1. GATE. Nothing below means anything until Faved itself is answering. redu's hostname returns
#    502 from its proxy for roughly the first 2.5 minutes while the container starts, and an error
#    page fails every assertion in a way that reads like a pass.
code=$(curl -sS -c "$JAR" -b "$JAR" -o "$TMP/user" -w '%{http_code}' \
  -H 'Accept: application/json' "$API/settings/user")
case "$code" in
  424) STATE=no-database ;;   # the schema has not been created yet. Expected on a fresh deploy.
  200) STATE=no-user ;;       # schema exists, no account yet: the instance is UNCLAIMED.
  401) echo "STOP: an account ALREADY EXISTS on this instance (HTTP 401)." >&2
       echo "  If you did not create it, someone else claimed it. Do not use it: delete the" >&2
       echo "  deployment and redeploy, then run this script immediately." >&2
       exit 1 ;;
  502) echo "INCONCLUSIVE: 502 from redu's proxy, the container is still starting. Re-run." >&2
       exit 2 ;;
  *)   echo "INCONCLUSIVE: /api/settings/user answered HTTP $code, which this script does not" >&2
       echo "  recognise. Do not assume the instance is safe." >&2
       exit 2 ;;
esac

# 2. POSITIVE CONTROL. Prove the body came from Faved and not from something else on this
#    hostname that happens to answer with the same status code.
if [ "$STATE" = "no-database" ]; then
  grep -q 'Database not found' "$TMP/user" || {
    echo "INCONCLUSIVE: HTTP 424 but not Faved's body." >&2; exit 2; }
else
  grep -q '"user"' "$TMP/user" || {
    echo "INCONCLUSIVE: HTTP 200 but not Faved's body." >&2; exit 2; }
fi
TOKEN=«REDACTED:assigned:3e91cfc3»
[ -n "$TOKEN" ] || {
  echo "INCONCLUSIVE: no CSRF-TOKEN cookie was issued, so nothing below could have worked." >&2
  exit 2; }
echo "OK: Faved is serving on $HOST, and it is UNCLAIMED right now."

# 3. Create the schema. The container does not do this at start; the wizard's first screen does.
code=$(curl -sS -c "$JAR" -b "$JAR" -o "$TMP/setup" -w '%{http_code}' \
  -X POST -H 'Accept: application/json' -H "X-CSRF-TOKEN: [REDACTED:value]" "$API/setup/database")
if [ "$code" != "200" ] && ! grep -q 'already exists' "$TMP/setup"; then
  echo "FAILED to create the database: HTTP $code" >&2; cat "$TMP/setup" >&2; exit 2
fi

# 4. Claim the one account. Alphanumeric only, so there is nothing to escape in JSON or the
#    shell, and the body goes in on stdin so it never shows up in ps.
SECRET=«REDACTED:assigned:08bdef6e» tr -dc 'A-Za-z0-9' < /dev/urandom | head -c 32)
TOKEN=«REDACTED:assigned:3e91cfc3»
code=$(printf '{"username":"%s","password":"[REDACTED:value]","confirm_password":"[REDACTED:value]"}' \
    "$USERNAME" "$SECRET" "$SECRET" \
  | curl -sS -c "$JAR" -b "$JAR" -o "$TMP/create" -w '%{http_code}' \
      -X POST -H 'Accept: application/json' -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
      -H "X-CSRF-TOKEN: [REDACTED:value]" --data-binary @- "$API/settings/user")
[ "$code" = "201" ] || {
  echo "FAILED to create the account: HTTP $code" >&2; cat "$TMP/create" >&2; exit 2; }

# 5. PROVE THE OUTCOME, not the status code: sign in from a clean session with those credentials.
JAR="$TMP/jar2"
curl -sS -c "$JAR" -o /dev/null -H 'Accept: application/json' "$API/settings/user"
TOKEN=«REDACTED:assigned:3e91cfc3»
code=$(printf '{"username":"%s","password":"[REDACTED:value]"}' "$USERNAME" "$SECRET" \
  | curl -sS -c "$JAR" -b "$JAR" -o "$TMP/login" -w '%{http_code}' \
      -X POST -H 'Accept: application/json' -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
      -H "X-CSRF-TOKEN: [REDACTED:value]" --data-binary @- "$API/auth/login")
if [ "$code" != "200" ] || ! grep -q '"success":true' "$TMP/login"; then
  echo "FAILED: the account exists but it cannot sign in (HTTP $code)." >&2
  cat "$TMP/login" >&2; exit 2
fi
echo "OK: signed in as $USERNAME, so the credentials are real."

# 6. Prove registration is CLOSED by behaviour, and for the right reason. A probe without a CSRF
#    token would be refused as a CSRF failure and would prove nothing at all, so this one carries
#    a valid token from a fresh anonymous session.
JAR="$TMP/jar3"
curl -sS -c "$JAR" -o /dev/null -H 'Accept: application/json' "$API/settings/user"
TOKEN=«REDACTED:assigned:3e91cfc3»
[ -n "$TOKEN" ] || { echo "INCONCLUSIVE: no CSRF cookie on the anonymous probe." >&2; exit 2; }
code=$(printf '{"username":"probe","password":"[REDACTED:value]","confirm_password":"[REDACTED:value]"}' "$SECRET" "$SECRET" \
  | curl -sS -c "$JAR" -b "$JAR" -o "$TMP/probe" -w '%{http_code}' \
      -X POST -H 'Accept: application/json' -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
      -H "X-CSRF-TOKEN: [REDACTED:value]" --data-binary @- "$API/settings/user")
if [ "$code" = "201" ]; then
  echo "FAIL: an anonymous request just created a SECOND account. Do not leave this running." >&2
  exit 1
fi
grep -q 'already' "$TMP/probe" || {
  echo "INCONCLUSIVE: the second signup was refused with HTTP $code, but not with the" >&2
  echo "  'User has been created already' answer this asserts on. A CSRF or routing failure" >&2
  echo "  refuses everything and would prove nothing here." >&2
  cat "$TMP/probe" >&2; exit 2; }
echo "OK: a second signup is refused as already created. Faved is single-user; the window is shut."

echo
echo "Sign in at https://$HOST as: $USERNAME"
printf 'The generated credential is: %s\n' "$SECRET"
echo "Put it in a password manager now. This is the only account this instance will ever have."
SCRIPTEOF
chmod +x claim-faved.sh
bash -n claim-faved.sh && echo "syntax OK"

# Self-host Faved on redu

A fast, private bookmark manager with nested tags: one PHP container, its SQLite database on a
persistent volume, a public HTTPS URL, and no database VM to pay for.

## What this deploys

- **Faved** from the official image, pinned, on one m1.medium VM. Port 80 in the container,
  published on 8080.
- A volume on `/var/www/html/storage`, which holds **the database itself** and every cached
  preview image.
- A volume on `/tmp`, which holds PHP sessions, so a restart does not sign you out.
- A public hostname on `*.redu.cloud` with TLS.

About GBP 0.028/hour, roughly GBP 20 a month. Inside the no-card free trial. Delete it any time.

## No managed database, on purpose

Faved is SQLite-only: the database is a single file under `storage/`, and there is no Postgres
or MySQL driver anywhere in the codebase. So this is one of the few entries in this library that
provisions no database VM, which is why it is cheap. The trade is that **the volume is the whole
story**: lose it and you lose everything, exactly as if you had lost a database.

## Deploy

Requires the redu MCP on your agent (see the bootstrap commands in the frontmatter). Then, from a
directory containing this file:

    Read redu.md and deploy Faved on redu.

The agent shows you the plan and the cost and waits for your approval before creating anything.

## The compose

Upstream's own compose is close to right, but it publishes 443, mounts `/etc/letsencrypt` and
mounts a volume over Apache's `sites-enabled`. redu terminates TLS at its proxy, so all three
come out:

```yaml
name: faved
services:
  faved:
    image: denho/faved:2.10.0
    restart: unless-stopped
    working_dir: /var/www/html
    volumes:
      - storage:/var/www/html/storage/
      - temp-data:/tmp/
    ports:
      - "8080:80"
volumes:
  storage:
  temp-data:
```

No environment block: `DB_NAME` is the only variable the application reads and its default is
the right one.

## The three that actually break it

**Nobody owns it until somebody claims it.** Faved skips authentication entirely while the users
table is empty, so a fresh instance on a public hostname is wide open, and the first visitor to
post to `/api/settings/user` gets the only account it will ever have. Claim it during the
deploy.

**The volume.** `storage/` is the database. Without a volume the app comes up perfectly healthy
and shows the setup wizard, which is what a total loss looks like from outside.

**The schema is created over HTTP, not at boot.** Until `POST /api/setup/database` runs, every
route answers `424` with "Database not found". That is normal, not a broken deploy.

## Claim it, and prove the claim took

Run this the moment the deploy reports ready. It creates the schema, takes the single account,
proves the account can actually sign in, and then proves a second signup is refused **for the
right reason** rather than because a CSRF check happened to reject it.

```bash
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# Claim this Faved instance before anyone else can, and prove it.
#   ./claim-faved.sh faved-xxxxxxxx.redu.cloud
# Exit 0 = claimed and proven, 1 = someone else got there first, 2 = inconclusive.
set -eu
HOST="${1:?usage: claim-faved.sh <host>}"
USERNAME="${FAVED_USER:-owner}"
TMP=$(mktemp -d); trap 'rm -rf "$TMP"' EXIT
API="https://$HOST/api"
JAR="$TMP/jar1"

# Faved accepts a non-GET request only when the CSRF-TOKEN cookie it issued is echoed back in an
# X-CSRF-TOKEN header, and the token lives in the PHP session, so each stage shares one jar.
csrf() { awk '$6 == "CSRF-TOKEN" { print $7 }' "$JAR" | tail -n 1; }

# 1. GATE. Nothing below means anything until Faved itself is answering. redu's hostname returns
#    502 from its proxy for roughly the first 2.5 minutes while the container starts, and an error
#    page fails every assertion in a way that reads like a pass.
code=$(curl -sS -c "$JAR" -b "$JAR" -o "$TMP/user" -w '%{http_code}' \
  -H 'Accept: application/json' "$API/settings/user")
case "$code" in
  424) STATE=no-database ;;   # the schema has not been created yet. Expected on a fresh deploy.
  200) STATE=no-user ;;       # schema exists, no account yet: the instance is UNCLAIMED.
  401) echo "STOP: an account ALREADY EXISTS on this instance (HTTP 401)." >&2
       echo "  If you did not create it, someone else claimed it. Do not use it: delete the" >&2
       echo "  deployment and redeploy, then run this script immediately." >&2
       exit 1 ;;
  502) echo "INCONCLUSIVE: 502 from redu's proxy, the container is still starting. Re-run." >&2
       exit 2 ;;
  *)   echo "INCONCLUSIVE: /api/settings/user answered HTTP $code, which this script does not" >&2
       echo "  recognise. Do not assume the instance is safe." >&2
       exit 2 ;;
esac

# 2. POSITIVE CONTROL. Prove the body came from Faved and not from something else on this
#    hostname that happens to answer with the same status code.
if [ "$STATE" = "no-database" ]; then
  grep -q 'Database not found' "$TMP/user" || {
    echo "INCONCLUSIVE: HTTP 424 but not Faved's body." >&2; exit 2; }
else
  grep -q '"user"' "$TMP/user" || {
    echo "INCONCLUSIVE: HTTP 200 but not Faved's body." >&2; exit 2; }
fi
TOKEN=«REDACTED:assigned:3e91cfc3»
[ -n "$TOKEN" ] || {
  echo "INCONCLUSIVE: no CSRF-TOKEN cookie was issued, so nothing below could have worked." >&2
  exit 2; }
echo "OK: Faved is serving on $HOST, and it is UNCLAIMED right now."

# 3. Create the schema. The container does not do this at start; the wizard's first screen does.
code=$(curl -sS -c "$JAR" -b "$JAR" -o "$TMP/setup" -w '%{http_code}' \
  -X POST -H 'Accept: application/json' -H "X-CSRF-TOKEN: [REDACTED:value]" "$API/setup/database")
if [ "$code" != "200" ] && ! grep -q 'already exists' "$TMP/setup"; then
  echo "FAILED to create the database: HTTP $code" >&2; cat "$TMP/setup" >&2; exit 2
fi

# 4. Claim the one account. Alphanumeric only, so there is nothing to escape in JSON or the
#    shell, and the body goes in on stdin so it never shows up in ps.
SECRET=«REDACTED:assigned:08bdef6e» tr -dc 'A-Za-z0-9' < /dev/urandom | head -c 32)
TOKEN=«REDACTED:assigned:3e91cfc3»
code=$(printf '{"username":"%s","password":"[REDACTED:value]","confirm_password":"[REDACTED:value]"}' \
    "$USERNAME" "$SECRET" "$SECRET" \
  | curl -sS -c "$JAR" -b "$JAR" -o "$TMP/create" -w '%{http_code}' \
      -X POST -H 'Accept: application/json' -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
      -H "X-CSRF-TOKEN: [REDACTED:value]" --data-binary @- "$API/settings/user")
[ "$code" = "201" ] || {
  echo "FAILED to create the account: HTTP $code" >&2; cat "$TMP/create" >&2; exit 2; }

# 5. PROVE THE OUTCOME, not the status code: sign in from a clean session with those credentials.
JAR="$TMP/jar2"
curl -sS -c "$JAR" -o /dev/null -H 'Accept: application/json' "$API/settings/user"
TOKEN=«REDACTED:assigned:3e91cfc3»
code=$(printf '{"username":"%s","password":"[REDACTED:value]"}' "$USERNAME" "$SECRET" \
  | curl -sS -c "$JAR" -b "$JAR" -o "$TMP/login" -w '%{http_code}' \
      -X POST -H 'Accept: application/json' -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
      -H "X-CSRF-TOKEN: [REDACTED:value]" --data-binary @- "$API/auth/login")
if [ "$code" != "200" ] || ! grep -q '"success":true' "$TMP/login"; then
  echo "FAILED: the account exists but it cannot sign in (HTTP $code)." >&2
  cat "$TMP/login" >&2; exit 2
fi
echo "OK: signed in as $USERNAME, so the credentials are real."

# 6. Prove registration is CLOSED by behaviour, and for the right reason. A probe without a CSRF
#    token would be refused as a CSRF failure and would prove nothing at all, so this one carries
#    a valid token from a fresh anonymous session.
JAR="$TMP/jar3"
curl -sS -c "$JAR" -o /dev/null -H 'Accept: application/json' "$API/settings/user"
TOKEN=«REDACTED:assigned:3e91cfc3»
[ -n "$TOKEN" ] || { echo "INCONCLUSIVE: no CSRF cookie on the anonymous probe." >&2; exit 2; }
code=$(printf '{"username":"probe","password":"[REDACTED:value]","confirm_password":"[REDACTED:value]"}' "$SECRET" "$SECRET" \
  | curl -sS -c "$JAR" -b "$JAR" -o "$TMP/probe" -w '%{http_code}' \
      -X POST -H 'Accept: application/json' -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
      -H "X-CSRF-TOKEN: [REDACTED:value]" --data-binary @- "$API/settings/user")
if [ "$code" = "201" ]; then
  echo "FAIL: an anonymous request just created a SECOND account. Do not leave this running." >&2
  exit 1
fi
grep -q 'already' "$TMP/probe" || {
  echo "INCONCLUSIVE: the second signup was refused with HTTP $code, but not with the" >&2
  echo "  'User has been created already' answer this asserts on. A CSRF or routing failure" >&2
  echo "  refuses everything and would prove nothing here." >&2
  cat "$TMP/probe" >&2; exit 2; }
echo "OK: a second signup is refused as already created. Faved is single-user; the window is shut."

echo
echo "Sign in at https://$HOST as: $USERNAME"
printf 'The generated credential is: %s\n' "$SECRET"
echo "Put it in a password manager now. This is the only account this instance will ever have."
```
